items.title: What a bad trip is and isn't: a "this is not X, it's Y" correction with lists
items.your_version: When too much hits you at once, your nervous system can become flooded, nothing makes sense, and we call it a bad trip. I might feel in the moment like  you're damaged for good, no that you're being punished for being spiritually impure. But more likely factors include the dose of what drug(s) you took and how your body handles them. Old painful memories could have been triggered, or you may have gone in with a fearful mindset, or the setting or people around you could have fed into it. Be kind about to yourself or to whoever's going through it, because blaming anyone only makes it heavier.

items.my_version: A bad trip does not prove that you are broken, punished, unspiritual, impure, or permanently damaged. It means the nervous system, meaning-making system, body, environment, memories, dose, or relationships became overwhelmed. The response is care rather than blame.

items.title: The day after: a run of short commands and don'ts
items.your_version: Don't make huge decisions or diagnose yourself from an intense night. You don't need to assume every vision was literal, nor that anything you realized is actually true (or false). Ask your body what it needs from you now. I'm  betting it will tell you: Give me sleep, natural food, pure water, a nice nature walk. It helps to integrate the experience via journaling your feelings, and talking with someone grounded (not the 20 chaotic people who are still coming down). To prevent your mind from giving spirituality a negative connotation, engage in some sober prayer or gentle meditation.

items.my_version: Don't rush to turn a hard experience into content. Sleep. Eat simple food. Drink water. Walk. Journal. Pray and meditate gently. Talk with one grounded person, rather than twenty chaotic people. Don't make huge decisions, diagnose yourself from one intense night, or assume every vision was literal and every fear was false. Let the system settle.
